card.hook: Two giant stone faces stare out of the sandstone at Želízy, each about 9 metres tall, and you can walk right up to them. The real challenge is getting both into one photo.
card.stand_here: Stand about 10 m west of the heads, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. You'll be looking straight at the rock faces, so keep your phone upright.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x so both heads fit, because you're only around 11 m away. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x or more (depending on your phone) to pick out the carved features.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the stone, then drag the slider down a little to make the shot darker if the sky is bright, so the carved detail doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: You're facing east, so afternoon sun will be behind you. Check how the light falls on the faces when you arrive, because the weathered texture looks best when the light isn't flat. Thin cloud helps too, as it softens harsh shadows.
card.selfie_here: Try the path climbing the hill just below the carvings (uphill from the parking area). Use the front camera at 0.5x and tuck the heads in over your shoulder. It's a loose tip, so check the angle when you get there.
card.rules_and_safety: The heads stand on private land, so check the official site for current access before you go. Please don't climb on the carvings, as visitors doing that damages them.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot with trees and rock for scale, then a tight shot of a single face, and keep your phone level so the rock doesn't seem to lean.
card.good_to_know: Sculptor Václav Levý carved the heads between 1841 and 1846. They're described as the second largest carved heads in the world, behind only Mount Rushmore. In 2011 the owner had the pine forest cleared, so you can now see them openly, even from the I/9 road. Nearby, the Harfenice (Harpist) and Had (Snake) reliefs make good extra frames.

selfie_research.notes: The pages do not name a clear spot where a visitor stands with the heads directly behind them; the selfie spots are inferred from photo and viewpoint tips, so check on arrival. The Locationscout tip ('up to the hill where they are') is vague. The viewpoint on top of the heads places the visitor on the landmark itself, not in front of it. The passer-by spot is based on pages saying the heads are visible from the street and, since 2011, from the I/9 road; neither page names a safe place to stand, and the I/9 is a main road, so a nearby side spot should be checked. A Random Times page says visitors climbing on the heads damages them, which is a conservation point, not a safety one, so I left the safety field empty. No page mentions selfie stick or tripod rules.

card.hook: Picture a forest path in the Czech woods, and then a stone Hussite leader staring out of the rock at you. That's Klácelka, a cave that's really a sculpture in disguise.
card.stand_here: Stand on the open forecourt below the rock face, right where the phone icon on the map sits. Face the rock squarely so the cave mouth is in the middle.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the cave mouth, the faces and the rock wall in one frame. If you're pressed against the far edge of the forecourt, drop to 0.5x. Then try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for close-ups of a single face or relief.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the carved faces so they stay sharp, then drag the slider to make the scene a little darker if bright gaps in the trees wash out the rock. Switch on gridlines too, so the edges of the rock stay straight.
card.best_time: Overcast days, or the soft light of morning and late afternoon, suit the sandstone best. Midday sun through the trees throws patchy shadows across the carvings.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the open ground in front of the cave portal, the area called Blaník. Use the front camera (or 0.5x if you have it) and stand near the carved Hussite figures so the sleeping army is right behind your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The cave is in a protected heritage area, so keep to the paths and don't touch the carvings. Sources disagree on access. One says the cave is closed because the reliefs were damaged, so you can only look inside through a barred iron door. Check on arrival or on the official site.
card.challenge: Can you fit Žižka, Holý and one grumpy dwarf into a single frame without cutting anyone's head off?
card.good_to_know: The young sculptor Václav Levý carved Klácelka in the 1840s. It's named after František Klácel, a theologian and philosopher. Levý turned the rock into an imagined Blaník, the hall where legendary heroes sleep, and the reliefs inside illustrate one of Klácel's fables.

card.hook: Two stone faces, each about 9 m tall, glare out from between the pines, and they're a lot bigger in person than you'd think. Around here, the Devil's Heads are the reason to climb out of the village.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the Čertovy hlavy, the two heads in the pine forest above Želízy. Follow the blue trail up from the village and face the carvings.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x so one head, the rock and the trees all fit in the frame. Switch to 1x for a more natural look. If your phone has 2x or 5x, use it for the faces and carved details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the stone, then slide it a little darker if bright sky shows through the trees.
card.best_time: Go on an overcast day or a calm morning, when the light is soft and the weathered stone looks its best. Patchy sun through the trees makes the faces hard to read.
card.selfie_here: Use the open clearing on the blue trail in front of the two heads, about 400 m up the path above Želízy. The forest there was cut in 2011, so you get a clear view of the sculptures behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, and keep a head over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Please don't climb on the carvings. The stone is fragile and climbing is already causing damage.
card.challenge: Can you frame one face between two pine trunks so it looks like it's peeking out at you?
card.good_to_know: Sculptor Václav Levý carved the heads in the first half of the 19th century. They are the largest work in a wider set of rock carvings around Želízy. If you have time, the nearby Harfenice cave has a faded relief of a woman with a harp.
